projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Tom Shimrock was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941 when war came to America?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: '41 I was living in Euclid. And, like everyone, of course, we start at the beginning.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Everyone who is alive remembers where they were and what they were doing when they heard that Pearl Harbor had been bombed. Yes, and my good friend, Charlie Bronick (ph), and I were sitting in the living room in our home with the radio on. Or actually, I was showing off. I was kind of showing off our new radio -- combination radio, record player, and home recorder, one of the first home recorders, and they announced that Pearl Harbor had been bombed. Nobody knew what Pearl Harbor was. I was 21 years old, and my friend Charlie was 21 years old. I looked at him and grinned, and I said, "Charlie, here we go." The war clouds had been gathering for years in Europe, and I expected that my generation would be involved in the war. Fact is, I started -- I started training -- here's a picture of me at the age of 15. I spent parts of three summers at Fort Benjamin Harris in Indiana in a part of the citizen's military training camp preparing myself for the inevitable. But I didn't rush in to join up right away, I waited a couple months. And it wasn't until Groundhog Day, February 2nd, 1942, that I made the rounds of the recruiting stations. But since I wore glasses, I couldn't meet the eye requirements. And so I thought, well, I knew they'd get around to me, and I sat around and waited. Draft Board was slow in getting around to me. When they finally did, the employer I worked for said all employees, when they get Draft Board notices, notify personnel, which I did. But turned out that they hired an attorney, an attorney who put pressure on Draft Boards to get their employees exempt. And much to my chagrin, I got a notice that I was deferred. I objected, I complained to the personnel -- personnel manager and complained to the Draft Board, and they said, well, nothing we can do, we made a contract with your employer. Well, that was that. Generally deferments were good for about six months. So I thought, well, I'll sit it out. Six months later I got another notice I was deferred again. Again I protested, but it didn't do any good. Well, okay, so I waited that six months and I got a third notice, deferred again. There again I went and complained. Draft Board wouldn't call me up, you're needed here for the defense effort and all that, so I quit my job. And took weeks before they finally called me up. When I finally went down, they called me, and went for the physical, I got the shock of my life. I was rejected for a heart condition. No one had ever complained about my heart. I felt -- I felt drained, like all my blood drained into my shoes or something. And I argued with the doctor, but -- doctors, they wouldn't approve me. So that was that. I left there at the examination station headed for the nearest phone booth and called up a heart specialist, and one of the leading heart specialists in Cleveland at the time, he took me right away, gave me a physical, took an echocardiogram, fluoroscope, checked me out. He said there's nothing wrong with your heart. Some doctors that aren't on their toes mistake a certain sound for a heart murmur. He wrote a letter to that effect that I still have buried here somewhere. I went back to the Draft Board and showed them the letter, but -- well, they weren't very much interested. They said, well, we have to have a release from your employer. The employer would not give a release, so it didn't do me any good. So I got another job for a few months. Finally they got around to calling me again, and I went again for the physical, this is about probably eight months later after the first time, and there again they rejected me for the heart. Four doctors -- it tied up the whole place. Four doctors tuned in on me and asked me all kinds of questions, had me bend over, hop up and down, did you ever have any heart problem, pain, any symptoms, no, I didn't have any. So they held a conference. Two said I was okay, and two said I wasn't. Well, the young doctor in whose line I was said, "You want in?" I said "Yeah," so he okayed me. But that wasn't the end of it. When there were about a thousand of us there standing in our birthday suits, when you came in they gave you a little four-by-six card with a large number on it. That was your number. Over the PA came a -- over the PA system came an announcement number 787 or something like that report to Room 101. Well, that was my number. I went there. The guy said, "Take a bottle off the shelf and fill it half full. Seems they found sugar in the urine." So they sent me to four days Columbus for observation. By this time they got wise to people kind of on the fringe where they go out and get boozed up before the exam and all kinds of things show up, so they were sending them for observation to get the true story on people's condition. I was given a glucose tolerance test, and much to my shock I was rejected for low blood sugar, which I didn't know I had. There again I was dejected and that was that. So I was resigned I couldn't get in. But after a year or so of laying around I decided I gotta go. Well, I guess -- oh, well, I guess I didn't tell you why I wanted to go, but I'll get to that. After about a year I decided I've got to go, I'm too -- I'm clever enough to figure out a way of going, to getting in. The Draft Board will not call me up because they had quota to fill, and anyone that was rejected they did not get credit for. I was 24 years old by now, so I had a scheme. I decided I'd get a Lake County address, change my age, and I'd go to Willoughby and register as an 18-year-old. So that's what I did, went in there, told them I just turned 18, here to register for the draft, which I did. Then I asked for immediate induction. You get a form to fill out stating you will not appeal any decision to the Draft Board. That's what I did. 30 days later I was in the Army. I guess -- well, I didn't tell you how I got in -- passed the physicals. I took my chances that the doctor would not find a fault with my heart because most of them never did. And to get by the sugar condition in the urine it's very easy, I just skipped breakfast on the day of the examination so there would be no sugar showed in the urine. So I was in the Army. I was sent to -- now this was -- I was inducted January 20th, 1945, shortly after the Battle of the Bulge, and I was shipped to South Camp Hood, Texas, as it is now Fort Hood, for -- they had a large infantry replacement training center. That word "replacement" had a certain ominous connotation. Okay, we had five -- about five months of basic training there, and they really drove us sometimes seven days a week. It was tough, but I help as good and even better than some of the others. Well, at the end of the five months we were all ready, and we were getting a 10 day delay en route they called it, not the furlough. We turned in all our equipment, we were about to board a train for home in about an hour, then they called -- out of my company of 250 they called off 10 names. I was one. Go get your equipment back that you turned in. For some reason, we don't know why, I was one of 10 selected for training to become cadre, and that's to train the other recruits. Well, that took about a month or so, I was not selected for a cadre. Went home, and -- Well, there was a 10 day, then was sent back -- sent to Camp Maxi, Texas for advanced infantry training. We suffered in the heat there for about six weeks and then sent to the fort in Washington outside of Seattle. I think it was -- oh, well, I keep forgetting the name. Laid around there for a while. Then they were -- we were sent to Fort Or -- Oregon, I think it was, which was the port of invocation, and we were all -- turned in all our uniform for new uniform, new equipment. We were given our overseas uniform. I was being fitted for my new outfit when the news came that the atom -- the bomb had been dropped. Well, of course, we did go on. I was sent to Hawaii, Oahu, and ended up in the prisoner of war compound there across from Wheeler Field near Scoffield Barracks there. There were several prisoner of war compounds there. We had Italian prisoners there, I think probably a couple thousand. Then after a few months they shipped them out somewhere and soon we got replaced by Japanese visitors. Well, I served my time there until I had enough points to leave, and that was it. I -- well, I -- yes, of course, I had to lie to get in, cheat my way in, but I'm proud of it. In fact, I brag about it. I guess we should have started at the beginning and why did I want to get in service. Well, because I was 21 years old. All my classmates -- my three brothers were in, all my classmates, all my schoolyard friends, every one of my -- practically every one of my generation was there. I knew it wouldn't be a great, happy time and a great adventure because I had training, had some military training and the basic, of course. I counted the ways we were trained, and I can think of about 15 different ways we were taught to kill and maim and blow up and incinerate and whatnot, and I knew that was part of the military and it wouldn't be a fun thing. I just wanted to be able to say -- I figured maybe some day I might be married and some day I might have kids, and some day if they asked me, "Dad, what did you do during the war," I'd want to be able to say I was there and I did my part. Now, there were -- there were probably hundreds of thousands of boys and men like me that had the same desire that wanted to get in. Every war there are boys that lie about their age, young boys that claim they're old enough to lie to get in. Every war that happens, but I don't think it very happens -- very often happens that someone like I reduced his age to get in, but it worked. And -- well, I know a former co-worker of mine -- in fact, I heard several cases like this -- was rejected for a hernia for the service. He went out and had his hernia repaired and then he ended up in the Navy. There have been a number of cases like that. I volunteer at Lake West Hospital, and recently I was talking to an 87-year-old patient, and his son and granddaughter were visiting with him, and still -- he said he was rejected for the service during World War II because of a punctured eardrum, and he said, "I cried all the way home." Someone that felt so strongly about it that he wasn't ashamed to say it in front of his son and granddaughter. On the other hand, there were school for draft dodgers. There were people who didn't want to. And, of course, when the draft was initiated, many hundreds of thousands of fellows suddenly found themselves madly in love and rushed off, got married to avoid the draft because, of course, the draft, they picked the single men first and then the married and no children, married and one, two, three children and so forth. Well, that's the reason I wanted to get in. Incidentally, my friend Charlie that was there at home when we heard about Pearl Harbor ended up in the Air Force, and he was shot down in Europe, and he was missing in action, and we were sure he was a goner. We hadn't heard from him in a year and a half. But when the war was over he surfaced. He escaped from the prison camp a couple times, and he ended up with the French underground but couldn't get word home. He made a career of the military. Well, let's see. I've got some notes here. You want to shut it down, review here? You asked if there were any memorable things in the training. There were several things that combined with my difficulty to get in I finally decided God just -- there must be a God, and for some reason he or she didn't want me messing around in any wars. With all the trouble I went to get into, and then I ended up -- there was an epidemic of measles in the camp, and I was the only one out of a company of 250 that came down with the measles that could have delayed my training. Well, I spent 10 days in the hospital and didn't get to learn how to handle mines. They were learning all about mines, which I never did while I was there. I'm not a sickly person, but I think I picked it up from the guy in the bunk ahead of me because he was a redhead, and spots wouldn't show on him like they did on me, and he complained about headaches for three days, and I think he had the measles and I must have got it from him. Well, I think that was just the good Lord trying to throw another road block in my path. Then why was I one of 10 out of 250 chosen to stay behind for more training? Later we heard that some of the fellows in basic training saw action in Okinawa. Well, there was -- then, too, in training the first time we handling -- learning to fire the mortar. Well, when you're first handling live ammunition you're kind of nervous about it. And we were waiting in line there, another young fellow from Chicago -- I was sitting waiting my turn just about four feet away, he had the mortar there, he was trembling with fear. And he mishandled the mortar in such a way that -- it's too complicated to explain here, but it was just a miracle that it didn't blow up and blow us up the way he did. There again I think the Lord was on my side for some reason. Well, that was one. There were other -- a couple other incidences. Well, there were -- I'll tell you about a few other people who -- well, I've already told you about the patient in the hospital that said he cried because he couldn't get in, several people like my other friend that had this hernia repaired to get in. Go back to World War I. Harry Truman didn't have to go. He was 31 years old, too old for the draft. He could have been deferred because he was a farmer and the sole support of his mother and sister. Also, he couldn't pass the eye test. But he volunteered and passed the eye test by remembering the eye chart. Now, I also did that. When I was trying to get in the service, I finally gave up and thought, well, I'll go to the Merchant Marine. Their requirements were same as Navy, but I passed their physical by remembering the eye chart. And I can tell you from memory the eighth line forward and backwards. Read the eighth line with your right eye forward and the eighth line backwards with your left eye, and I can tell it from memory right now. I passed the eye test. But when they found out that I was 4F, had been rejected for the service, that was the end of that, they wouldn't accept me. Also beside Harry Truman, I read the poet Robert Service during World War I. His friends were in the service, and he wrote this, "When they come back, if they come back, shall I not be ashamed to be among them." He then became an ambulance driver in France. That's the way so many of us felt. Well, that's pretty much it. So here I am, a veteran, and proud of it. That's pretty much my story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it frustrating for you before you finally got in, was it frustrating, did you have to keep explaining to people why you were a single man?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Oh, sure. Yes, on the job, yes, people wondered and sometimes aloud.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you getting anxious that you were afraid it would end before you'd get in?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Oh, no, no, no. No, I wasn't worried about that. I just wanted to get in and say I served. And to say I volunteered was an understatement.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies that you went through training with?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: I never -- no, we all went our different ways. I never kept contact with any of them. We all come from many different states, and they're separated in training. I stayed behind and the others went their ways. No, I just -- I often wondered what happened to many of the others, where they ended up, but never in contact.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't keep in touch with the ones that were shipped over when you stayed behind?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Huh-uh. One of my brothers -- all four of us brothers were unmarried. One of my brothers was snapped up at the beginning of the draft. And, you know, it was supposed to be for 12 months, drafted only for a year. He ended up five years in the service. There was a popular song then was, "I'll be Back in a Year Little Darling." Well, that year stretched into five years for him. Yes, and -- let's see, that rang a bell on something else. Oh, yes, about wanting to get in, another popular -- very popular song during those years was a country singer named Elton Britt recorded a song -- what in the heck is it? Oh, gosh, I know it well, but I can't think of it now.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I'm going to throw a couple titles at you because I have some. There's a Star Spangled Banner Waving Somewhere?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Right, right, Star Spangled --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I'd Like to Give My Dog to Uncle Sam?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Yeah, that was it, the Star Spangled Banner Waving Some -- yeah. It was about a poor mountain boy.

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About the guy that was in jail that wanted to get in the service?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Oh, probably they would all wanted to change their position with a chance in the service, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But he did a number of songs like that about guys trying hard to get in.

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Yeah. Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other details or memories of Army life during your training time, anything at all?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Well, yes, I did -- when I was in Hawaii they have an inspector general -- representative of inspector general comes around to listen to your gripes and things. Well, by then the shooting was over, and I didn't felt there were much of a need for me, and I did go and I tell him that I lied and cheated to get in the service and I want to get out. Well, he listened and presumably made a record or it, but nothing ever became of it. And also after I got out of the service several years later I went to the VA office there in the Republic Building I think it was -- Cuyahoga Building in Cleveland, the VA was there, and I went in there and told a guy there that there were some discrepancies in my record and I want to straighten it out. He said, "What did you do, lie about your age?" And I said, "Yeah." He said, "I wouldn't bother with it." So you see I -- so I didn't. But he presumed I was probably a young fellow and said I was older. Well, it doesn't matter, but he said, "I wouldn't bother. I'd let it go." So okay, I let it go. So I did make two attempts to straighten it out. But then, yes, you say were there any memorable things. Okay, when I was assigned to the prisoner of war camp there I was a messenger. I picked up messages at -- mail or messages at the headquarters at Scoffield Barracks and delivered them to several of the military Army posts in Hawaii in Oahu. Well, we were agitating -- there were a lot of agitating -- the GIs wanted to get home. In fact, there was a big demonstration there in Fort Shafter -- no -- yes, Fort Shafter there in Hawaii, and a couple followed me, showed up demanding to be shipped home, and the Army -- the military claimed they didn't have the ships and all that. But anyway, go back to -- well, I was just as anxious as the others to get back. Like I say, I felt there was no need, I wanted to get back and resume my civilian life. But when I picked up the messages one day at -- deliver it to the other outpost I read one the orders. And the commander there, it was a General Smith, and this is what he said. I had to read it a couple times to believe it. "Regardless of any" -- let's see. "Regardless of any action enacted by Congress or any" -- "Regardless of any legislation enacted by Congress or any legislation now pending, the basis of separation from this command will be X number of points and/or X number of years." So what he was saying is he was going to defy -- he was going to defy the Government of the United States, and he was going to run his command the way he wished. These generals, they didn't want to lose their men, they wanted to sit on their thrones there. But that was unbelievable. I got so damn mad about it that I typed up a letter -- there again, you send it to the inspector -- you send your gripes to the inspector general. I typed a letter up citing this plus another gripe and sent it airmail special delivery to the Inspector General, Washington, DC. Well, the minute I dropped it in the slot I felt kinda foolish, and I was sure nothing would become of it. Well, but about a month later the first sergeant came over one day and he said, "You and Captain Hughes (ph) are to report to Fort Kam in Honolulu at headquarters" -- I said okay -- "in the morning." I said, "Well, what for?" He says, "Oh, I don't know, something about some letter you wrote." So okay. So the captain and I went there, and I was interviewed by a representative of the inspector general, and they had a court reporter there to take out -- to make a note of everything that was said. And, well, the first lieutenant there said -- he had my letter including the envelope it was sent in and half a dozen papers stapled to it. Well he said, "Looks like you really started something here." He said, "Your letter went all the way up to General McArthur and all the way down the chain of command to here for me to investigate." I thought he was just blowing air. Well, I was interviewed there, and I stated my position and my gripes. And then they interviewed the captain. I wasn't there. But riding going back to the camp he said, "Gosh," he said, "your letter went all the way up to General McArthur." And I said, "It did?" The lieutenant said, "That's what I thought he was just talking." He said, "No, I saw the letter from McArthur to investigate this complaint." So I got a laugh out of that. So sometimes it does pay to -- Oh, yes, that's right, I decided if the general had his way I would have another eight months to stay in the service, and I didn't want to stay in the outfit I was in, I wanted to get in the Air Force which was right next door, and there even the garbage collectors had stripes there, you know, sergeants. And I thought, well, so I want a transfer. Well, when the -- that was one of the things I wanted in my letter. And after my interview was over the lieutenant says, "Well, I think we can arrange a transfer." But I said no thanks because by then I knew when we were going home. I said, "No thanks, I don't want it now." But that was an interesting little incident that happened. I chuckle about it. So sometimes it does pay to complain or if you've got a legitimate gripe. That's -- outside of that I can't think of any.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Aside from that, did you enjoy your time being stationed in Hawaii?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: It was nice there, but there's no place like home. Yes, it's nice, but as -- several times we requisitioned the Jeep and we'd go on a Sunday and just drive around the island. The maximum -- we were able to -- you could drive around the whole perimeter of the island was 110 miles. And as one of the fellows said, "Back home we drive further than that just to see a ball game." It was nice, but you want to get back, resume your life. That's pretty much it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good. Any other vivid memories come to mind about anything either on the home front? Do you have memories of when you were on the home front before you got in about rationing or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yes, there was rationing. It was no big thing. I had whatever they had

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Felt you got enough to eat, that wasn't a problem?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Oh, yeah, there was no problem.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bootlegs et cetera?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: I can't -- no, I can't think of nothing. We were proud. There were three or four of those stars home that had servicemen or women in the service, they had little towel-like things with stars on there indicating how many went in the service, and we had three stars hanging in my window. Our window.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your parents go along with it the whole time you were trying to get in, or did they try to talk you out of it and say you don't have to go?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Well, I don't know -- I really don't remember what my dad said, but I know my mother said -- tried to -- said don't go, don't go, but I wanted to go. Don't have any regrets. It was a good experience, yet -- yeah, the -- one interesting thing that happened after -- after basic training, you know, I told -- wrote my girlfriend I'm coming home. I didn't -- that was before I was called out to pick up all the equipment I turned in because I was staying there for further training, and she had a party set up, everyone -- everyone was there. They all had a good time, everyone was there except me. Well, it turned out she took up with one of the fellows that was at the party and married him. But that was probably all for the better. Then I got one of these proverbial Dear John letters that were common during the war, you know, when you're separated, Dear John letters, and boys are up in the front and the wife back home says, I got boyfriend now or I got married or so forth. Well, it's kind of hard to take for a while, but I know -- I knew then and I know now it's for the better. It was the right thing. And that was interesting. She picked up a husband at my party. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was it a good reunion when you finally got back home, when you finally got out?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: No big reunion. I've always been somewhat of a loner, you know, I never belonged or have a -- except in my younger days I was kind of leader of the pack in junior high and had a lot of friends there, but after a while -- no, I just resumed life, tried to find a job. That's pretty well my story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's your story.

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Incidentally, I never -- I never applied for any benefits, you know, that -- I didn't milk the VA for benefits of any kind. Almost nothing. So I didn't --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't want to go to school on the VA or do anything like that?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Well, I figured -- I didn't -- I come from a very poor family, and we didn't have -- I didn't have the resources. And I figured to go to college, I'd be 31 years old when I got out of college, you know, and I didn't want to do that. Well, that's pretty much it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But, yeah, it's amazing, it's great, because any point there you could have said -- mine's still on, is yours? At any point there you could have said, you know what, this isn't going to happen, I'm just going to go to work and forget about it, but it's great that you wanted to keep -- you kept trying.

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: Well, I needed -- for my ego, you know. Yeah, it was an ego thing pretty much. And every place I go practically all the ones my age are there that were in the service. In fact, normally at this time there are about six of us co-workers meet every Tuesday at 12:00 at the Food Court in the Great Lakes Mall, and we sit and chew the fat, but all were in service, including the one that had his hernia repaired so he could get in the Navy. Everyone was in the service. I would have been the odd ball. Everywhere -- seems like almost every place I go I would have been the odd ball, the one that wasn't in the service. Interesting thing my friend Charlie that I mentioned at the very beginning, I didn't -- I didn't see much of him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Especially to help out a flier. I mean, I had heard that their reaction to our guys that were bombing them was not so good, but perhaps at that point in the war --

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: I know one of my other classmates was tail gunner in the -- in Europe there, and they were told if they were shot down don't -- if you have a choice, don't surrender to the home guard because they'll kill you, surrender to the military. That was interesting too. You pick up a lot of these little tidbits.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Tom Shimrock
sp.p: That pretty much covers it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's very good. I have to say I've talked to close to a hundred Veterans, and this is a very unique story.
